tagline: Stone walls and tree canopies lead from farm fields to ocean
intro: The Paradise Loop winds through southeastern Middletown on Aquidneck Island, linking narrow farm roads with Second Beach and the Sakonnet River. Tree canopies and stone walls enclose parts of the drive; elsewhere, fields and coastal water open the view. Rhode Island designated Paradise Avenue and Associated Roads in May 1993. RIDOT highlights the historic houses, mature roadside trees, rock formations and shoreline along the designated network.

Paradise Avenue was originally nominated on its own, before the rest of the loop was added. The countryside had already drawn carriage riders from Newport and nineteenth-century painters to Paradise Valley. The 2003 stewardship plan made preserving agricultural uses and open scenery a central aim, alongside coordinating the loop’s historic and recreational places. Stone walls and scattered farmsteads preserve evidence of eighteenth-century field patterns, even where later summer houses and residential subdivisions changed the roadside.

Travel counterclockwise from Wyatt Road onto Berkeley Avenue, passing Whitehall before Berkeley becomes Paradise Avenue. Continue beside the Maidford River to Second Beach, then follow the coast beneath Hanging Rock into woodland. Indian Avenue brings views across estates and fields toward the Sakonnet River. Turn west on Peckham, then follow Wapping Road, Mitchell’s Lane and Wyatt Road through the agricultural side of the loop.
notice: Rough fieldstone boundary walls contrast with the more formal stonework along Indian and Paradise avenues.

moments.title: Whitehall
moments.text: Crafted stone walls mark the entrance to Whitehall, the farmhouse George Berkeley enlarged to his own design. He bought the farm and its small house in February 1729 while working toward a college planned for Bermuda. Berkeley also purchased enslaved people to work the land. When he left in 1731, he donated Whitehall and his library to Yale, stipulating that income from the property support three scholars. Yale leased the property as an inn for many years before its late-nineteenth-century decline into dereliction. In 1899, the Colonial Dames obtained a 999-year lease; in 1936, they commissioned restoration of two rooms.

moments.title: Second Beach
moments.text: At Paradise Avenue’s meeting with Hanging Rock Road, the view opens south toward Narragansett Bay and the Purgatory Chasm bluffs. St. George’s Gothic chapel stands on the hill above the road. The chapel opened in 1928, designed by Ralph Adams Cram and donated by alumnus John Nicholas Brown. Along Hanging Rock Road, the landscape includes marsh grasses, beach plum and rosa rugosa. Beyond the beach, open coastline gives way to a narrower, curving road between the bird sanctuary and Gardiner Pond Reservoir. The transition places the beach, wetland vegetation and reservoir within a single stretch of road, before the route enters Indian Avenue’s residential landscape.

moments.title: Hanging Rock
moments.text: Hanging Rock overlooks beaches, ocean and reservoir from within the Norman Bird Sanctuary. The view appears in paintings by John LaFarge, and George Berkeley made frequent visits during his stay in Middletown. The water landscape below has changed: beginning in 1889, dredging and diking nearly doubled Gardiner Pond for use as a reservoir. The enlargement removed marshy margins that had expanded and contracted with the pond’s natural water level. The sanctuary itself grew from a farm and was founded in 1949 through Mabel Norman Cerio’s bequest. The sanctuary contains hay fields, woodlands and ridges overlooking the ocean and ponds.
